_: german-fixes.json — the record of every hand edit to a German (`goethe`) deck, applied by german-fix.js (its header has the format). `insert`: cards a deck's list lacks — a new card (senses from the English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, each sentence a Tatoeba sentence named by its German and English ids in the third place) or a card MOVED from another deck (`fields`, byte for byte, with `from`). `notes`: fields rebuilt on a card a deck already has. `decks`: `dropDup` (a card a lower deck carries), `dropForm` (a card that is only a form of another), `subtitle` and `descSub`. Every entry says why.

goethea1.why: No German deck carded du: Goethe A1 had dich and dir, and the pronoun table on every pronoun's card, but no card for the commonest word of address. Meaning: English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16 (du, pronoun). The All-forms panel is the ich card's own table. Sentences: Tatoeba, by id.

Zero was in no German deck as a number: the Wortgruppenliste counts from eins, and German B2 cards null as the adjective (null and void). Meaning: English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16 (null, numeral). Sentences: Tatoeba, by id.

goethea1/ja.why: The card gave only the modal particle (obviously; certainly; of course), so English → German asked for ja with 'obviously' and the word for yes was nowhere. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: ja, interjection (yes; yea; yeah; aye) and adverb. Two sentences replaced with short ones; the third is the card's own.
ex: Oh mein Gott, das ist ja mein Haus!
Oh my God, it's my house!

goethea1/aber.why: The card gave only the adverb (rather; quite; unusually) over three sentences of the conjunction. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: aber, conjunction (but; however; though) and adverb.
ex: Tut mir leid, aber das ist einfach unmöglich.
I'm sorry, but that's simply impossible.

goethea1/Sie.why: All three sentences were of sie (she, they), and the gloss 'you' is shared with four other cards. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: Sie, pronoun.
ex: Excuse me, what is your name?

goethea1/ihr/ihm/ihn.why: The headword was the list's line ihr/ihm/ihn, the meaning that of ihr alone (you; ye) and the three sentences of ihr as her and their, so no card taught the plural you. Renamed ihr (the id is kept); ihm and ihn stay in the pronoun table of the All-forms panel. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: ihr, pronoun (you, ye (plural, familiar); dative of sie) and determiner (her; their).

goethea1/heißen.why: All three sentences were of the adjective heiß (heißen Kaffee, heiße Wetter). Sentences: Tatoeba, by id.

goethea1/nein.why: Two of the three sentences were of 'ne and na, not nein. Sentences: Tatoeba, by id; the third is the card's own.
ex: Nein, ich bin es nicht, du bist es!

goethea1/für.why: The second sentence marked vor, not für. Replaced with a Tatoeba sentence; the other two are the card's own.
ex: Mach's, wie du es für richtig hältst.
Sie gaben Georg die Schuld für das Versagen.
They blamed George for the failure.

goethea1/hallo.why: The first meaning was Wiktionary's sub-gloss (a general greeting used when meeting someone) without the word it explains, so English → German never asked with 'hello'. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: hallo, interjection (hello: a general greeting …).
senses: a general greeting used when meeting someone
an initial response when picking up a phone call

goethea1/die Entschuldigung.why: The word a beginner says is the interjection, which the card did not give, and its second sentence marked Entschuldigungen in 'Entschuldigungen Sie'. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: Entschuldigung, interjection (excuse me, pardon, sorry) and noun. Two sentences from Tatoeba; the third is the card's own.
ex: Er hat für sein Benehmen um Entschuldigung gebeten.

goethea1/bitte.why: The card gave the adverb alone; the answer to danke is the interjection. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: bitte, adverb (please, if you please) and interjection (you're welcome; excuse me, sorry; here you are).
senses: excuse me, sorry (request to repeat information)

goethea1/best-.why: The card carried gut's meanings (good; all right; fair) and a 'not gut' hint, so it taught best- as good. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: beste is the superlative degree of gut. The sentences are the card's own.

goethea1/gut.why: The 'not best-' hint goes with the best- card's borrowed meanings; the meanings are unchanged.

goethea2/meinen.why: A sentence was of the possessive (meinen Schirm). Sentences: Tatoeba, by id.

goethea2/weg/weg-.why: The generator took the informal adjective (unconscious; passed out; hammered) and found no sentence. English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: weg, adverb (away; gone, not there). Sentences: Tatoeba, by id.

goethea2/der Schweizer, die Schweizerin.why: The generator took the proper noun (a surname). English Wiktionary via kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16: Schweizer, noun (Swiss person, Swiss (male)); Schweizerin (female Swiss).

descSub: The cards are ordered by roughly how often a word is used, so the ones you meet most often come first. The measure is one scale for every deck here:

THE ORDER is by what a reader can already read: first the 281 expressions spelled entirely with words and forms Goethe A1 shows, then those that need A2 (136), B1 (192), B2 (100), C1 (38) and C2 (9), and last the 209 that use a word or a form no German deck here shows (most often a word of the idiom alone). So the first part can be begun beside Goethe A1: at the default pace of ten new cards a day, five expressions, they take 57 days and the whole deck 193. The greetings and first sentences (guten Morgen, auf Wiedersehen, wie geht's, ich heiße and six more) are cards of Goethe A1 and are not repeated here. Inside each part the expressions come by roughly how often they are used. The measure is one scale for every deck here:

The cards are ordered roughly by how common the word is in everyday German, so the words you meet most often come first: the order is taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles, with a phrase — which a list of single words cannot see — placed by how often it turns up in a corpus of everyday sentences.

THE ORDER is written for someone starting from nothing. The first 87 cards are laid out by hand: the greetings and courtesies (hallo, guten Morgen, danke, bitte, Entschuldigung, ja, nein), a first exchange (ich bin …, wie heißt du?, ich heiße …, wie geht's?), the subject pronouns, ten verbs, the question words, zero to ten and the commonest function words. After that the words come roughly by how common they are in everyday German (a frequency list built from film and television subtitles), with each closed set kept together — the days of the week from card 151, the colours from 201, the numbers above ten from 251, the months and the seasons from 351 — and a noun and the word spelled like it (das Essen, essen) forty cards apart. AT THE DEFAULT PACE of ten new cards a day — both directions of a word together, so five words a day — the first 87 cards take eighteen days and the whole deck takes 160 days. A deck cannot set that pace itself: to finish sooner, raise the new cards a day in the deck's options. NOT ON THE EXAM BOARD'S LIST: twelve of these cards — du and null, which no German deck carded, and ten courtesies and first sentences that stood in the phrases deck (guten Morgen, guten Tag, guten Abend, gute Nacht, auf Wiedersehen, wie geht's, es tut mir leid, vielen Dank, ich heiße, wie heißt du). HOW A WORD IS READ is the subject of German — Sounds and spelling, which is meant to be studied beside this deck; Goethe A2 follows it.
Each of the 156 verbs carries its full paradigm
